newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Dollar to see return of volatility in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Dollar to see return of volatility in 1997.

text.p: Volatility in dollar currency markets, an absent feature for much of 1996, looks set to return in 1997, foreign exchange analysts say.

Continued uncertainty over the gathering momentum of Europe's monetary union and its effect on the dollar, toppy U.S. asset markets and a far from certain interest rate outlook all point to a choppy year ahead.

"This uncertainty next year is going to be a key feature and may be a reason why volatilities pick up from their current very, very low levels," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
Some economists said fairly benign underlying economic factors as well as well-sychronised global growth and monetary policy should lead to further currency stability.
SENTITIVITY TO EMU PLANS

But Meggyesi anticipated that current uncertainty, particularly the market's hypersensitivity to Europe's path to monetary union, could bring greater volatility than the economic environment warrants.

Apart from a brief upward blip in recent weeks, dollar/mark one-month implied option volatility has declined steadily from just below 12 percent this time last year, touching historic lows just above six percent in recent months. The picture is much the same for dollar/yen options.

"There is an expectation that volatility will increase next year which will be welcome boost for the currency options market," said an options trader at U.S. bank. "There has been some long-dated dollar call buying but this air of uncertainty has also dampened any aggressive plays so far."
The biggest variable and volatility hotspot remains Europe and the dollar's reaction to economic and monetary union (EMU).

"The single most important factor driving the dollar is EMU expectations," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan in London. "It's not the Federal Reserve, it's not interest rates, it's a belief that the euro will arrive and will replace the mark and will not be as strong as the mark which is benefiting the dollar".
STABILITY PACT BOOSTS DOLLAR

The stability pact negotiated last weekend has put Europe that much closer to a single currency. Because of the compromise made to achieve the pact and the door it opens for Europe's peripheral currencies on first-wave participation the dollar is finding support, at least for now.

"The mark is going to suffer and the dollar is going to go stronger against the continental currencies, there is no doubt about that," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.
"The problems are stacked up and continuing to stack up for the mark because the German economy is assumed to be weaker and the nearer the euro comes the greater the risks for the mark."

Lyons sees a significant mark depreciation next year with the dollar moving closer to 1.70 marks from around 1.5450 at present, a level he stresses will be attributed to German weakness rather than a rosier scenario for the U.S. economy.

JP Morgan's Persaud is also bullish on the dollar's prospects and sees the dollar heading towards the 1.65 level and dollar/yen around 115-120, from around 113.80 at present, in the next three to six months.
The latest Reuter poll of banks' and financial institutions' currency forecasts indicated a dollar/mark level of 1.5459 and dollar/yen at 109.79 in twelve-months time.
INVESTORS SEEK HIGH-YIELDERS

"The key factor will be a global interest rate environment of low rates in core countries, encouraging investors to sell marks and yen to look for EMU convergence trades in Europe and go to more high yielding currencies outside," said Persaud. "The U.S. isn't a high yielder but it generally benefits in that kind of environment."
The U.S. economy will also play its part for dollar direction, but analysts say this influence will be relatively minor as bullish economic influences neutralise the bearish.

The bullish dollar scenario of economic growth with the possibility of the Federal Reserve tightening is seen by some as being tempered by expectations of a continued recovery in the German and Japanese economies next year.
Also, higher U.S. rates in the near term could have a negative impact on U.S. asset markets which have so far played a large part in the recent dollar strength.
A growing U.S. trade deficit is also seen as a potential drag on the dollar. So far, this has not proved a problem for the currency but analysts are wary of an ever-widening trade gap.
"If the deficit continues to widen then this will become an issue in itself and the risk premium for the dollar will increase, putting some downward pressure on the currency," said DMG's Meggysi.
ANALYSTS URGE PATIENCE

On the plus side, the risk of the Clinton administration bowing to domestic calls for a more competitive dollar is seen as being low with only a sharp slowdown in the economy precipitating any explicit policy shift towards a weaker dollar.
While dollar volatility is expected to increase next year, some analysts caution that some patience may required.

"It will be a year of two halves. The first like 1996 with low volatility, a trending dollar and good flows to high yielders," said JP Morgan's Persaud. "I think the second half is where the action will be and then we'll see why we need options traders."
